title: Power and energy bills
ks3: Energy: power, kilowatt-hours and the cost of energy at home
intro: How fast do your devices use energy, and what does it cost? Practise power in watts, energy in joules and kilowatt-hours, and working out electricity bills.
description: Free KS3 Physics power and energy bill questions with answers: watts and kilowatts, energy = power × time, kilowatt-hours, meter readings and the cost of electricity. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: What does the power of a device tell you?
options: How much energy it can store
questions.hint: A more powerful kettle boils water faster.
questions.explain: Power is how much energy is transferred each second. 1 watt means 1 joule every second.

questions.q: What is the unit of power?
questions.hint: It is named after James Watt, who improved the steam engine.
questions.explain: Power is measured in watts (W). Energy is measured in joules (J).

questions.q: A 60 W bulb is on for 10 s. How much energy does it transfer? (Energy = power × time)
questions.hint: 60 W means 60 J every second.
questions.explain: Energy = 60 W × 10 s = 600 J.

questions.q: A kettle transfers 24,000 J of energy in 10 s. What is its power?
questions.hint: Power = energy ÷ time.

questions.q: A phone charger has a power of 5 W. How much energy does it transfer in 1 minute?
questions.hint: Change 1 minute into seconds first.
questions.explain: 1 minute = 60 s. Energy = 5 W × 60 s = 300 J.

questions.q: Two hairdryers are the same except for their power. Which one transfers energy faster?
options: They transfer energy at the same rate
questions.hint: Power tells you how many joules are transferred each second.
questions.explain: 1800 W means 1800 J every second, and 1200 W means 1200 J every second. The bigger the power, the faster energy is transferred.

questions.q: A microwave oven has a power of 1000 W. You heat some soup for 2 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?
questions.hint: Change 2 minutes into seconds, then use energy = power × time.
questions.explain:
2 minutes = 120 s.
Energy = power × time = 1000 W × 120 s = 120,000 J.

questions.q: A 2000 W kettle needs to transfer 300,000 J of energy to boil some water. How long does it take, in seconds?
questions.hint: Energy = power × time, so time = energy ÷ power.
questions.explain: Time = energy ÷ power = 300,000 J ÷ 2000 W = 150 s (2 and a half minutes).

questions.q: How many watts are there in 2.5 kW?
A 2 kW heater is on for 3 hours. How many kilowatt-hours does it use? (kWh = kW × hours)
questions.hint: Multiply the power in kW by the time in hours.
questions.explain: 2 kW × 3 h = 6 kWh.

questions.q: A 100 W TV is on for 5 hours. How many kilowatt-hours does it use?
questions.hint: Change 100 W into kW first.
questions.explain: 100 W = 0.1 kW. Energy = 0.1 kW × 5 h = 0.5 kWh.

questions.q: What does a kilowatt-hour (kWh) measure?
questions.hint: It is the unit on an electricity bill. Is a bill for how fast, or for how much?
questions.explain: A kilowatt-hour is an amount of energy: the energy a 1 kW device transfers in 1 hour. Power (how fast) is measured in watts or kilowatts.

questions.q: A 200 W games console is used for 3 hours. How many kilowatt-hours does it use?
questions.hint: Change the watts into kilowatts first.
questions.explain:
200 W = 0.2 kW.
Energy = 0.2 kW × 3 h = 0.6 kWh.

questions.q: How many joules are there in 1 kWh?
questions.hint: 1 kWh is 1000 W for 1 hour. How many seconds are in 1 hour?
questions.explain:
1 kW = 1000 W and 1 hour = 3600 s.
Energy = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3,600,000 J. That is why bills use kWh: joules would give huge numbers.

questions.q: Electricity costs 25p for each kWh. How much do 8 kWh cost, in pence?
questions.hint: Cost = number of kWh × price of one kWh.
questions.explain: 8 × 25p = 200p, which is £2.

questions.q: A 3 kW oven is on for 2 hours. Electricity costs 25p per kWh. How much does it cost, in pounds?
questions.hint: Find the kWh first, then the cost in pence, then change to pounds.

questions.q: An electricity meter reads 01234 kWh on Monday and 01264 kWh on Friday. How many kWh were used?
questions.hint: Subtract the first reading from the second.

questions.q: From Monday to Friday a home used 30 kWh. Electricity costs 30p per kWh. What did that cost, in pounds?
questions.hint: 30 × 30p, then change pence to pounds.

questions.q: Electricity costs 25p per kWh. One wash in a washing machine uses 2 kWh. How much does one wash cost, in pence?
questions.hint: Cost = number of kWh × price of one kWh.
questions.explain: Cost = 2 × 25p = 50p.

questions.q: A 2 kW tumble dryer runs for 1.5 hours. Electricity costs 30p per kWh. How much does it cost, in pence?
questions.hint: Find the kWh first (kW × hours), then multiply by the price.
questions.explain:
Energy = 2 kW × 1.5 h = 3 kWh.
Cost = 3 × 30p = 90p.

questions.q: A 10 W LED bulb is left on for 100 hours. Electricity costs 25p per kWh. How much does that cost, in pence?
questions.hint: Change 10 W into kW, then find the kWh, then the cost.
questions.explain:
10 W = 0.01 kW.
Energy = 0.01 kW × 100 h = 1 kWh.
Cost = 1 × 25p = 25p.

questions.q: Which of these is a good way to save energy at home?
options: Switch off lights when you leave a room
Open the windows with the heating on
Swap LED bulbs for filament bulbs
questions.hint: Which one stops energy being transferred when it isn't needed?
questions.explain: Switching off lights stops energy being used when nobody needs the light. The others all waste energy.

questions.q: Each device is switched on for 3 minutes. Which one transfers the most energy?
questions.hint: For the same time, the device with the biggest power transfers the most energy.
questions.explain: Energy = power × time. The times are the same, so the kettle, with the biggest power (2000 W), transfers the most.

questions.q: Which transfers more energy: a 2 kW kettle on for 6 minutes, or a 10 W LED bulb on for 10 hours?
questions.hint: Work out the kWh for each. 6 minutes is 0.1 hours and 10 W is 0.01 kW.
questions.explain: Kettle: 2 kW × 0.1 h = 0.2 kWh. Bulb: 0.01 kW × 10 h = 0.1 kWh. The kettle transfers twice as much, even though it is on for a much shorter time.

questions.q: Both bulbs give the same amount of light. Which one uses less energy in an hour?
questions.hint: For the same time, a smaller power means less energy.
questions.explain: The LED bulb has the smaller power, so in the same time it transfers less energy: 10 J every second instead of 60 J.

questions.q: Heater A (2 kW) is on for 1 hour. Heater B (1 kW) is on for 3 hours. Which uses more energy?
questions.hint: Work out kW × hours for each heater.
questions.explain: Heater A: 2 kW × 1 h = 2 kWh. Heater B: 1 kW × 3 h = 3 kWh. Heater B uses more, even though its power is smaller, because it is on for longer.

questions.q: An electric shower has a power of 9 kW. You cut your shower from 10 minutes to 5 minutes. How many kWh do you save?
questions.hint: You save 5 minutes of showering. Change 5 minutes into hours (a fraction of 60 minutes).
questions.explain:
5 minutes = 5 ÷ 60 = {1/12} of an hour.
Energy saved = 9 kW × {1/12} h = 0.75 kWh.
